Content: The problem with the comparisons is that there exists a baked in and gradual degradation of software from the OEMs. The budget phones if properly optimized can handle the cameras and everything like a flagship but if the budget one does that then why would people buy flagships?? The mobile ecosystem needs some rules and standards for software quality and maintainability like we have IP rating for water and dust protection. There needs to be a standard for software which clearly indicates the optimization level of the software corresponding to each version of the software and how the optimization gets affected by incremental updates of the OS. This will help users get phones from brands that focus more on providing an optimized experience to the user without making them feel bad for not having money while at the same time encouraging OEMs to invest more in making a product more reliable and robust.

Non-gaming vs. Advanced Gaming for Flagships
Standard (one-camera) Photography vs. Advanced Photography and Videography for Flagships

Hands haven't gotten bigger and, largely, neither have wallets.

Author: @HyperbolicMedia
Content:
TL;DR. I own the A36 at $320 and personally optimized it runs great almost like an older flagship. Score can also depend on personal dev access and tuning capabilities to a phone. 

I have the A36 i bought tax and all about $300 its basically the same as the 56. The 56 isnt for sale in the U.S. oh btw its not so much totally the AI but also the R.A.M and C.P.U processing and how they handle it. Not that you cant turn dev mode on and piddle your settings if you know what you're doing to make the midrange work as nice as the flagship in terms of snap. Ive edited my A36 to run similar to the S25 even at the lower basic 60hz refresh rate. Custom dev optimization has squashed what used to be 30GB of data to like 6.5GB. My multi window runs wonderfully my R.A.M isnt taxed and i get 4-6 years of software and security support. I had some bloatware but I deleted it all and disabled what I can. Runs fucking clean. Gemini is great on my phone. Grok also works nice but his servers are on the Fritz. I managed to make the A36 run really close to flagshipe without piddling with the internals. I'll warn. It does overheat nomatter how you have it set. Settings wise my cameras are a bit older but optimized in app to create nice photos even with the kinda grainy ×10 zoom. Stabile and everything. Very very similar to the A56 specs. Playing with the settings you can personally optimize how it runs. Battery run time is the only thing i cant optimize on the A36 unlike the S25. The A series is basically last years flagship but without all the optimization. Also though ironically my A36 runs a 60W charge. 125 risks eating the lithium reaction too fast 60-75 runs peak performance balance. End of the day id say i run around 25-30%. Charged a bit slow unless cooled.

Author: @jb678901
Content:
There is another option...buy the previous year's flagship model (NEW) at a discount to the current/latest flagship model.  I did this recently with an upgrade to the OnePlus 12 (16GB/512GB).  Literally half the price of the Samsung Galaxy S25+. I avoided nearly $300 premium for the latest OnePlus 13.
That OnePlus 12 came with screen protector installed, a RED USB A-C cable, and a 100W fast charging brick.
Are there compromises...of course.  IP65 vs IP68/69.  Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 vs Gen 4. No silicon-graphite anode tech within the battery (5400mAh vs 6000mAh).  
However, mine immediately upgraded to latest OxygenOS 15, has the same screen tech, and with the latest software tweaks...arguably a competitive camera vis a vis the OP13.
If you value the latest and greatest specs...go for the most current flagship option.  However, for my use case, the decision to go with the OP12 was a no brainer.
If on a tighter budget, that Redmi phone does offer some really compelling specs.

PS: The curved screen on the OP 12...which used to be a POSITIVE upgrade...has somehow become OLD tech.  This I do not get.  We have a very fickle media that clearly is pushing a common message from "somewhere"....like the fashion industry.

Author: @wesgregg6451
Content:
Samsung has been "a bit" slow on OS releases on most of its phones, the last couple of them. Android 15 was released in October, 2024. Some other cell phone companies are like that, to greater or lesser extent. I've always found this to be interesting. The OEMs have a limited number of models and hardware configurations, all of which must meet certain requirements in order to be certified for the OS to begin with. Meanwhile, linux OS distros have to be able to run on basically any combination of hardware components that the hardware users can come up with (and the vast majority of same was never created with linux OS users in mind, unlike the stuff in cell phones running Android - which was intended for Android... only), the developers are mostly unpaid volunteers instead of salaried employees... and things flow rather quickly. Even more, people are able to easily install linux on hardware that is three, five, even ten or more years old.

The primary reason for this difference is, I suspect, that the developers of Android must be financially incentivized to force users to buy new hardware on a regular basis.

Content: Ironically enough, I could easily get away with the mid-ranger you were showing here except for one little issue for me. Author: @danielamdurer1779
Content:
I see five tiers rather than three, and think you've compared tiers 2, 3 and 5.

1 - True Budget. Price point sub-£200 (often sub-£150), significant limitations are acceptable here.

2 - Upper Budget. The £300 range. Sometimes called "lower midrange", and one of the sweet spots for price.

3 - Midrange. £500 or so, often better than that Samsung, but still far from premium. The Pixel A series lies here.

4 - Sub-premium. Used to be £600, probably more like £800 today. Often the top of lesser-known brands, this is where flagship killers lie. Probably also a sweet spot for price.

5 - Premium. Over a grand. Modern features, top-end everything, setting the trends.

There might also be an ultra-premium, but I think Google are just taking the piss with their Pixel 9 Pro Fold.

Author: @dkursada
Content: Nowadays we pay for software optimization and added longevity from brands. Hardware-wise, gaps are narrow. It's the flagship killers that frustrate me a lot. Now they're handicapped by being given ugly bezels or having awful thermal performances and become a laggy mess constantly. Old flagships were such a good alternative despite having limited availability and issues from age or storage. The thing is, old flagship route is worth it only if you have a chain that offers good refurbished deals in where you live. Else, you'll see that second hand sellers jacking up the prices of old flagships, making that alternative not so worth it. So, consumers in most third world countries are left with the import route, which also has caveats depending on how their govt rulings handle imported devices. In short, smartphone space of 2025 rarely offers downright awful devices but it also rarely gives your money's worth since not having a critical weak point is what defines the luxury in those devices.

Author: @anthony23ant
Content:
As a proud owner of Poco X6 Pro, I wouldn't consider the Redmi Note 14 Pro+ 5G as a budget phone, it's a lower midrange,
Budget phones are the $100-$250 range to me. This 14 Pro+ is indeed in the range of $300 but my $237 X6 Pro performs leagues better than it, in sacrifice of cheaper build material and maaaaaybe camera

But as you also brought up in the video, the Xiaomi 14T is about $20 cheaper than the Samsung Galaxy A56, but the 14T is superior in almost every way
Better chip, bigger and faster storage, brighter screen, more versatile camera (obviously, since the Note 14 Pro+ is already better than A56) faster charging with charger included, and so on, the A56 only surpasses on it's Victus 2 (as oppose to 14T's GG5) and better IP rating (68 as oppose to 67), it has newer android (15 as oppose to 14) and Aluminum frame (as oppose to the mentioned plastic frame) which I would argue on a day to day usage, 14T's inferior parts won't be apparent or even noticeable, the 14T is cheaper and better than the A56 overall

Price doesn't always translate to performance and value, it's merely how the company wanna leech the customer, and I think Xiaomi's method of cutting the cost down while adding ads on the software to make up the missing revenue is brilliant, proven by how most of their phones are cheaper and better than other brands. This brand is still the king of price-to-performance ratio on almost every price range.

Edit: What I'm saying is basically these phones aren't a good representative of their respective price range, the Note 14 Pro+ is a shit all-rounder for the price, the A56 got dunked on by literally any other phone on it's price, and the S25 Ultra while it's never wrong to be a flagship, chinese brands have cheaper flagships (Xiaomi 14 Series, Oppo Find X8 Series, Vivo X200 series, the list goes on)

Author: @paultasker7788
Content: When it comes to used flagships the phones tend to end up being worth what they really are. An s24u for example is not that much cheaper than an s25. Still 700 to 800 pounds. Whereas a pixel 8 pro is a lot less. 420 for a 512gb version. Cheaper than an s23u! For the price of a midranger you can get a flawed fairly new last gen flagship. You get all the really nice flagship touches, excellent cameras, lovely haptics, top notch screen, and good AI. But why so cheap? Because the tensor 3 chip is only midrange. It's not that efficient and can stutter in some apps. Occasionally gets warm too. The modem is not that great although in the UK mine is par with anything else. In the US ive heard its pretty bad. Depends on what bands you use. Google tends to update it very often and some updates make it worse. The next one will likely fix it. Im not saying unusable but slower, hotter, worse battery. I was a beta tester and the phone on android 15 beta one was outstanding. Better than the current stock version. However beta 2 and 3 were poor and 16 beta nearly unusable so i went back to stock only to find still not as good as beta 1! Is google now really focusing on optimisation for the 9 series phones? I like to have a backup device and got a cheap Motorola 50 neo. In many ways its nicer. Feels smoother in some apps like YouTube, runs cooler. Camera has more modes. But haptics, camera quality, and speaker quality plus some neat touches show the difference and once google fixed a buggy update it is back in my pocket. For the price it is now (about 350) its some bargain so long as you accept its weaknesses. Performance and battery are not flagship but they are not terrible. You'll get 5 to 7 hours screen on time over a day and quite good in games. Just a little stutter when doing stuff like reading YouTube comments. Feels more app optimisation (mad as google owns it!) than raw performance as my Motorola scores 1/2 of the score in benchmarks.

Content:
Great concept, but poor execution. Many of the differences between the midrange and budget phones were not due to their price, but rather the fact that one was made by a Chinese OEM and the other by Samsung. Chinese phones generally have better specs on paper (e.g. 120W charging, better chips, large batteries, 200mp cameras, the latest gorilla glass, more premium materials, etc) at the cost of a lackluster software experience (less software support, less optimization, less battery life despite larger batteries, ads galore, etc). 

If the video had been comparing a Chinese budget vs a Chinese midrange vs a Samsung flagship the midrange phone would have been much more appealing for the price.

Author: @harshil.18
Content: I’m personally pretty disappointed with this Mrwhosetheboss video. I’ve watched him over the years put in a lot of effort to make his videos polished, interesting and fun. The problem with this video is it can’t be objective to a viewer watching it to find out how much value they are deriving for their money being spent or someone just watching how the technology landscape (smartphones to be specific) is at different price points. Based on my understanding of the technology landscape that I have developed over years of watching tech reviews, podcasts, et cetera is that flagships are usually good in every department, midrangers are either balanced or try to excel in a few areas, budget phones try to fulfil basic needs and usually cut costs to be competitive in pricing. The fundamental issue hindering this video’s objectivity is that you can’t compare flagships, midrangers and budget phones by picking one phone from each price category. To make the case for my argument, there is a brand called Nothing which apart from number of yearly updates (software support) has budget phones and midrangers beating even many flagship phones. Chinese companies have been providing large battery sizes due to battery technology innovations and fast charging speeds which disproves the section of this video that said that the budget phone in this video has a larger battery sizes than midrange and flagship phones. That was because he chose a Samsung phone for midrange and flagship. That’s a brand issue not a price point issue. Different brands have different priorities and cater to their customer’s needs in ways that reflect their vision. To make this video more objective and helpful, you need to look at many different phones from different brands in every price category and assign points to specific phones. Or maybe if you want to keep things simple, you can pick one brand for example Samsung and compare their budget, midrange and flagship offerings. I hope Arun you are taking note of this for future videos.

(The only meaningful difference here may actually be that the Redmi has already been on sale for a while, so it already has the cheaper market price, whereas the Samsung is currently still in the pre-order phase. Content:
Redmi is Chinese, and the Chinese have lower production costs due to paying workers less, and government owning parts of their business - making facilities and everything pay less taxes and generally be cheaper.

They're also doing it to get into the market, make the stuff good and cheap so that people go for it. They're still gonna be cheap, but if they gain more of a share in the market the prices will go up a bit. Huawei did the same thing way back, started with damn good phones for dirt cheap and raised their prices after me coming more mainstream. They ware still cheap and incredible, but their prices did go up.

I'm excited to see this evolve, if it forces the other brands to lower their prices later on to compete or if the Chinese brands gain popularity. I still stick to Samsung, but that's because I can't go to my provider and get a Chinese branded phone included with my plan. Where I live, I pay ~50usd a month for my S25+ with full coverage if it breaks or I loose it. And I can swap it in for another phone after 12/24 months. If I paid for a phone flat out and just paid for my plan it would be abt 30usd for the same plan with unlimited databand full speeds ect, so it's not even worth doing so. After the downplay period I don't even pay the full price of the phone, because the resell value is subtracted. And if I keep the same phone I still just pay for my plan and not any more on the phone.

If Chinese branded phones ware in available in those plans, I'd definitely try one out! Huawei was my fav brand, but after us banned it, the EU really stopped importing them and I went to Samsung after that and been sticking to them ever since. I almost went for a pixel instead this time, since I work offshore and wanted the cract good reception the pixels have, but I went with Samsung due to my galaxy watch and Samsung smart tags. Author: @Kirkaig
Content:
As a tight arse at heart who has both used budget-midrange Xiaomi and Samsung phones as well as their flagships (although Xiaomi was still in the price range of midrange) it's shocking what the differences are. 

There's so many cheap things that Xiaomi does that's amazing, first of all was the utility of the budget/ midrange phone. I had an IR blaster, headphone jack, dual Sim, and an SD card slot. As well as the software which has a built in ability to get any app you have installed as its APK, this includes any modded apps and it doesn't just "download" it, it's completely offline so no matter what the app is you can get an APK file of it. It's just so convenient and I found so many other just convenient and what would be cheap uses. 

For the Samsung flagship I can't seem to find many (if any) cheap features, they're not upgraded but it simply seems like they skip any cheap features that would just make it so much better. Since this includes software it also means their midrange/ budget phones are worse since they don't contain the advanced stuff or cheap stuff when it comes to software and no IR blaster. I love the s-pen and all the other advanced features but I want them to include the simple stuff, they also got rid of the LIDAR sensor which I despise them for as I'm really into 3D design and while photogrammetry has come a long way a LIDAR sensor is still useful. 

It seems that somehow the pure existence of Apple literally does the opposite of what more competition usually does. They're somehow egregiously expensive while getting as minimal as they can and consumers are stupid enough to buy that crap that it almost forces other companies to make their products worse because apparently it's what people want.

Having the Moto G5+ and G8+ near their release dates they were solid mid-range experiences. They had great cameras for the price and time period and never felt like much of a compromise.

Having a Moto G Power as a budget phone, while the features are fine, the camera was poor and the phone was just slower than molasses. I still have this phone but I cannot bare to use it as a daily driver.

Having a Samsung S21FE near it's release date felt like a premium experience. The performance was fantastic, the features were great. For about 2 years I was completely satisfied until the battery began to degrade to a range where I needed multiple charges per day.

Having now the iPhone 16 Pro Max gives me everything I liked about the S21FE and what was the best battery in a flagship phone at date of purchase. Not sure if the S25U is better or not. 

I would still be okay with a G5+ or G8+ equivalent phone in todays world given the camera were to meet a certain standard. I think the Redmi fits that bill very well. Since I use my phone for work however, I need to know I have the flagship performance so I am not slowed down on the day to day. 
I would likely be fine with a phone half of the price of the iPhone 16 Pro Max such as the S24FE, but the opportunity arouse and I decided to try the cutting edge. I don't think I need it but I have no reason to trade down. I'll have this phone for many years to come where as the longevity of a mid-range phone is to be debated.

Author: @geraldmcmullon2465
Content:
Last summer I had to purchase a newer phone so that the app to control my "smart speakers" would install. Having an Xperia XA1 I looked at the Xperia 1 VI and 10 VI. I couldn't justify the difference in cost for the flag ship model £1299 to the budget £349. Part of my wants included having a microSD slot and a 3.5 mm headphone jack. 

In Autumn I got a Samsung A15 for a friend as being more affordable than a basic iPhone. The Samsung has three lenses (50Mp, 5Mp, 2Mp; 13Mp selfie) to the Xperia's two (48Mp, 8Mp; 8Mp selfie) but the recording is 12Mp. The Samsung is slightly larger, slightly heavier and 2340 x1080 to 2520 x1080. Whether the difference of £220 is worth it I have my doubts. The software support and upgrades for 5 years from Samsung compared 2 is possibly the more important consideration. 

The biggest difference in use is the way the Samsung behaves compared to the Sony. The buttons and the onscreen pop ups do not behave the same and the internet proved harder than expected to track down why. I felt the same when trying to find options on an iPhone and iPad with the menu and layout very different to the help found on the internet. I guess that is why people stick to Android or iOS and even to a particular brand of Android phone. We can get used to any change but why bother?

Author: @justthisweeb
Content:
Not gonna lie I don't think the a56 is the best example of a midranger here 
Mostly because while it is a decent phone it's definitely far from the best midranger (I would say it's more of an all-rounder than most other midrangers but not really the best especially when it comes to performance)
For example in terms of performance there are a decent number of midrangers out there that just outclass it such as the poco x7 pro which released this year and is significantly cheaper (mostly due to cost cutting when it comes to materials and cameras but then again I'm talking about pure performance)
In terms of cameras, build quality, etc. there are just better midrangers that suit whatever the buyer actually wants to see in their phone (for example people who only really care about the good performance for stuff like games and don't care about cameras will probably not want the a56 over more performant phones and on the opposite end people who want better cameras but don't really care about performance so long as it's acceptable would choose a phone with better cameras)
In my opinion midrangers are the more "specialized" phones made for people who don't want to spend the money for a flagship and have specific needs but don't quite care about whether or not the phone is a good all rounder (as per my previous example people who just want to be able to game will easily be able to do so with more performant midrangers without spending the extra $800 for a flagship)
from my observations of the mobile market most people fall into the category of simply not caring about anything in particular about their phone and for them a budget phone or a more general midranger like the a56 (if it was cheaper) would be perfect as they don't care about whether they can take professional grade photos, ai, performance in games or anything in particular so long as they can scroll through social media, make calls and send texts
people who have a specific need they want fulfilled but are on a tighter budget would probably want to go for a midranger because it's not a whole lot more expensive than a budget phone but usually you can find phones that would meet a particular need 
and then finally people who just want the best of the best and don't care about the price would go for the flagship which is what I would personally call the result of all midrangers combined with more software support and the newest soc instead of a 1 or 2 year old one 

in my eyes they're basically just entirely different markets which can't really be compared properly
